austin-ecosystem-map-for-international-f.title: Austin ecosystem map for international founders
austin-ecosystem-map-for-international-f.description: A peer sketch of Station Austin, Capital Factory naming, IFN meetups, and how newcomers get warm intros without inventing a partner directory.
austin-ecosystem-map-for-international-f.html:
A founder who moved to Austin three weeks earlier walks into the building at 701 Brazos St on a Tuesday evening and asks the front desk which room the founder meetup is in. The answer is "which one?" There are several events that night. They find the IFN room, sit down, and the first thing they ask the person next to them is how anyone figures out who is who in this city.

That question comes up often enough that it deserves its own post. This is a peer sketch of the rooms international founders tend to pass through in Austin, and how newcomers turn cold arrivals into warm introductions. Not a program directory. Not a ranking.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, tax, immigration, or investment advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. Organizations, membership products, and program details change. This post does not endorse any program, investor, or service provider beyond the partners named below. Check current details directly with them before you act.

The building most people mean

When Austin founders say "let's meet downtown," they often mean 701 Brazos St.

The venue IFN uses for its monthly meetup is Station Austin (styled STATION Austin on its own site), at stationaustin.org. Station Austin is powered by Capital Factory. In 2026, Capital Factory spun out STATION Austin as a nonprofit to carry the community and programming side of the work.

You will hear people use both names for the same address. Someone who has been in Austin for years may say "Capital Factory" out of habit, while someone newer says "Station." If you are meeting someone there, confirm the address and the floor or room, not just the name.

Capital Factory still comes up when people talk about investment and the accelerator history tied to that building. If those conversations matter to you, ask people who have direct experience rather than relying on secondhand summaries.

Who is in the room

On any given evening, the building might host several meetups at once: industry groups, technical communities, investor office hours, and founder circles. Think of these as other rooms in the same building. Some will be useful to you and some will not. Founders who have been through it suggest sampling a few, then picking two or three to attend regularly instead of trying to be everywhere.

The IFN monthly in-person meetup is the room focused on international and immigrant founders. People there tend to share a specific set of problems: forming a US company from abroad, banking without US credit history, status questions, building a team across time zones, and explaining all of that to customers and investors. You will hear a mix of accents and home markets, and a lot of "I had that exact problem last year."

Peers in the room are usually at different stages. Some are still deciding whether to incorporate. Others are hiring their first US employee or preparing to raise. That spread is useful, because the person two steps ahead of you usually remembers the details of the step you are on.

Partners you will see around IFN

IFN works with a small number of partners. You will come across them in and around the meetup:

  • Station Austin is the venue partner and the coworking home for many founders in the community.
  • Reuneo runs speed networking at IFN meetups. The format puts you in short, structured conversations with several people in a row, which helps if walking up to strangers is not your strength.
  • Yani Partners is a technology partner for founders. (No public website to link here.)

That is the verified list. If you hear someone claim a formal IFN partnership that is not on it, ask an organizer before assuming.

How warm intros actually happen

Newcomers often expect warm intros to come from a perfect pitch or a polished LinkedIn profile. Peers describe something much plainer.

Show up more than once. The first meetup is mostly about faces. By the second or third, people remember your name and what you are working on. Most useful intros happen after a few repeat visits.

Ask one concrete question. "Does anyone know a good accountant?" gets polite nods. "Has anyone here opened a business account for a Delaware C-corp without an SSN, and what did the bank ask for?" gets three people leaning in. Specific questions are easy for people to answer, and easy to pass along to someone who knows more.

Use the speed networking. The Reuneo rounds at IFN take away the awkward part of starting a conversation. Use them to find the two or three people worth a longer follow-up, not to collect as many contacts as possible.

Follow up once, with context. After the meetup, send one short note: where you met, what you talked about, and one specific thing you would appreciate. Peers say a single clear follow-up works far better than a string of vague "let's grab coffee" messages.

Offer something back. Even newcomers know things others need: a home market, a supplier, a hiring channel, a language. The founders who get the most intros tend to make intros too.

What to skip in the first months

Some patterns waste newcomers' time:

  • Attending every event in the building in your first month and leaving with a stack of contacts and no relationships
  • Asking investors for meetings before peers who have raised have seen your story
  • Treating every logo on a wall as an endorsement. Hosting an event in a building does not make an organization a partner of everyone else who meets there.

When we stop talking

The room helps you find people. It cannot vouch for professional services on your behalf.

  • If an intro leads to a legal, tax, or immigration engagement, do your own diligence on that professional
  • If a program, accelerator, or investor offers terms, have qualified counsel review them before you sign
  • If you are unsure whether a connection or event affects your immigration status (for example, what activity your visa permits), ask an immigration attorney

Soft next steps

Come to the next IFN meetup with one concrete question about who you are trying to meet and why. Guests are welcome; register on Luma or check dates on ifn.community. If you want the private member channel and members-only call, Become a member. Curated intro norms and community notes live with membership and the Resources hub as that catalog fills in.

Sources

  • Station Austin, stationaustin.org
  • Reuneo, reuneo.app

building-your-first-50-connections-in-au.title: Building your first 50 connections in Austin from zero
building-your-first-50-connections-in-au.description: Meetup-first networking for international founders new to Austin: where peers start, how they follow up, and what backfires.
building-your-first-50-connections-in-au.html:
A common first night at the IFN meetup goes something like this. A founder walks into Station Austin knowing nobody, picks up a name tag, and spends ten minutes near the wall pretending to read their phone. Someone asks what they are building. They explain it badly, then better the second time. By the end of the evening they have talked to six or seven people and forgotten most of the names. They have written down two that matter: a founder who opened a US bank account last year with the same company structure, and someone who sells to the same kind of customer back home. That is two follow-ups, and it counts as a good first night.

This is peer orientation from that room. It covers how founders build a working local network from nothing: where people start, what they do after the first conversation, and what tends to backfire. It is not a networking playbook.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, tax, immigration, financial, or hiring advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. Introductions made at events are between the people involved. IFN does not vet the service providers, vendors, or advisors you meet there. Check credentials and official sources before you rely on anyone.

Why fifty, and why it stays loose

Fifty is a loose target, and nobody in the room is counting. What matters is the definition. A connection here means someone who would answer a message from you and remember who you are. A LinkedIn acceptance does not count, and neither does a business card left in a jacket pocket.

Founders who have been in Austin for a year or so describe the same shift. Once you have a few dozen of those relationships, the city starts to feel smaller. A question about a landlord, a payroll provider, or a first enterprise customer gets a fast answer because you know who to ask. Before that point, every question feels like starting from scratch.

Some people get there in a few months. Others take longer because they fly home often or keep late hours for a team in another time zone. Both are normal.

Meetup first

Most peers describe the same order: in-person rooms first, online second. Online works well for keeping a connection warm. It is a slow way to start one, especially when nobody here knows your name yet.

The IFN monthly in-person meetup for international and immigrant founders happens at Station Austin, 701 Brazos St. It makes a good first room because everyone there has dealt with some version of your situation: a company formed from abroad, a bank asking for unusual documents, a visa question that shapes what you can do. You do not have to explain why things are complicated. If you are new to IFN overall, Welcome to the IFN blog covers what this space is for.

Station Austin hosts other founder events in the same building through the month. After one IFN meetup, you will often recognize people at those too, and a second conversation with a familiar face moves faster than a first one with a stranger.

The room keeps coming back to one habit: bring one concrete ask to each event. "I am looking for a bookkeeper who has worked with companies that have a parent abroad" gets you a name. "I am trying to meet people" gets you a polite nod. A specific ask also gives other people an easy way to help, and that is how a lot of these relationships start.

Reuneo rounds at the meetup

IFN meetups use Reuneo for speed networking. You get short, structured conversations and rotate through several people in a set block of time. For newcomers, this removes the hardest part, which is walking up to a stranger.

Peers treat those rounds as a filter. A few minutes is not enough to settle anything. You are looking for two or three people worth a longer conversation later, over coffee or a call. Jot a quick note after each round about why someone stood out. By the end of the night the faces blur together, and the note is what you will use.

Follow up once, and make it specific

Most first conversations die at the follow-up. Founders who build their networks steadily tend to do three things. They write within a few days, while both people still remember the conversation. They mention something specific that was said, so the message could only have come from them. And they offer something before asking for anything.

Offering is easier than it sounds when you are new. You know a home market that most people in Austin know little about. Real offers include a short note on how customers buy in your country, an intro to someone back home, or a resource that helped during your own company setup.

Then follow up once. If it goes quiet, let it go. People are busy, and the next meetup gives you a natural second chance. Fuller notes on follow-up habits live with membership.

Three layers worth building

It helps to notice which kind of connection you are short on.

Peers a step ahead. These are founders who did what you are about to do six to eighteen months ago. They remember the details that official pages leave out, such as which document a bank actually wanted. In the first year, these tend to be the most useful relationships.

People in your industry. This means customers, potential partners, and operators at companies in your space. Austin has deep clusters in some sectors and thin ones in others, so ask the room where your people gather instead of guessing.

Service providers. You will meet plenty of lawyers, accountants, bankers, and vendors at events. Meeting someone at an IFN event does not mean IFN endorses them. Peers ask founders who have actually hired them, check licensing where it applies, and get scope and fees in writing before any work starts.

What tends to backfire

Sending a LinkedIn request to everyone on an attendee list is the mistake peers mention most. It feels productive, but it mostly produces a list of strangers who will not recognize your name.

Pitching in the first minute is close behind. Asking about someone's work, or what brought them to Austin, usually leads to a better pitch later because by then they want to hear it.

Collecting badges also catches people out: four events a week, a stack of cards, and no follow-up on any of them. One event a week with two real follow-ups tends to build more.

When we stop talking

Peer intros are a starting point. Bring in licensed help when any of these come up:

  • An intro turns into a contract, partnership agreement, or reseller deal
  • Someone offers you equity or advisor shares, or wants to invest
  • You are about to hire or contract someone you met, especially across borders or if your status limits what you can do
  • Money will move between your home-country entity and your US company as part of a new relationship

Corporate counsel, immigration counsel, and a CPA with cross-border experience each cover different questions.

Soft next steps

Come to the next IFN meetup with one concrete connection question: a kind of customer you want to meet, a service provider you are trying to find, or a peer who has done the thing you are about to do. Guests are welcome; register on Luma or check dates on ifn.community. If you want the private member channel and members-only call, Become a member. Fuller notes on follow-up habits and local founder rooms live with membership and the Resources hub as that catalog fills in.

Sources

  • Station Austin, stationaustin.org
  • Reuneo, reuneo.app

first-90-days-in-austin-as-an-internatio.title: First 90 days in Austin as an international founder
first-90-days-in-austin-as-an-internatio.description: Housing, neighborhoods, documents, and local ops peers at IFN Austin talk through so the company survives landing.
first-90-days-in-austin-as-an-internatio.html:
Austin's in-person meetups often have one founder holding a phone with a map open, asking the room which part of town they should actually live in. They landed two weeks ago. The company is formed, the bank account is half open, and they have spent their first ten days in a short-term rental. They are trying to work out whether to sign a twelve-month lease before they know where they will spend most of their time. Someone across the table laughs, because they asked the same question a year earlier.

This is peer orientation from that room: where people live, which documents everyone ends up scrambling for, and how to keep the company running while your personal life is still in boxes. Not a relocation checklist. Not a substitute for counsel.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, tax, immigration, housing, or banking advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. Lease rules, fair housing questions, tax residency, and status limits change with your facts. Verify with licensed professionals and official sources before you act.

First weeks versus first 90 days

Founders who have been through it describe two different jobs.

The first few weeks are about landing. You need a place to sleep, a working phone number, a way to get around, and a mailing address that will still be valid next month. Most people underestimate how much of this depends on documents they left in a drawer back home.

The first 90 days are about making sure the company survives the move. Payroll, invoices, bank logins, registered agent mail, and investor updates all keep going whether or not you have furniture. Peers who struggled usually let the company side drift while they sorted out housing, then spent a month catching up.

A pattern the room keeps returning to is to treat these as three separate tracks:

  1. Personal landing (housing, phone, transport, your own ID and paperwork)
  2. Company paper (entity, registered agent, state filings, contracts)
  3. Money rails (business banking, payment processors, how money moves between your home country and the US entity)

They overlap, but they break in different ways. A lease delay should not hold up a payroll run, and a bank asking for proof of address should not stop you signing a customer. Keeping the tracks apart in your notes makes it easier to see which one is actually stuck.

Housing patterns peers talk about

Nobody in the room will hand you a ranking of neighborhoods, and you should be wary of anyone who does. What you will hear instead are patterns.

Short-term first, lease second. Many founders start with a furnished short-term place for a month or two, then sign a longer lease once they know where they will spend their days. The trade-off is cost and some instability against making a twelve-month commitment before you know the city.

Roommate or solo. Some newcomers share a place with another founder or a professional they meet through the community, which can make lease approval easier when you do not have US credit history. Others need a quiet solo setup for late calls across time zones. Both are common. The right choice depends on your work hours more than anything else.

Neighborhoods people mention. A few areas come up again and again in conversation, each for its own reasons:

  • Downtown, near Station Austin at 701 Brazos St. Walkable to coworking, meetups, and a lot of daytime meetings. People mention it when they want to live close to where the founder community gathers.
  • East Austin. Founders bring it up for residential streets, cafes, and proximity to downtown.
  • North Austin and the Domain side. It comes up among people who work with larger tech employers up north or want more space.
  • The South Congress corridor. People mention it for its own neighborhood feel and easy access back into downtown.

Prices, availability, and how people feel about each area change. Talk to people who live there now before you decide. Bring your actual constraints to the meetup (car or no car, how often you need to be downtown, budget range) and you will get far more useful answers than "where should I live?"

Documents people scramble for

Almost everyone in the room has a story about a document they did not think they would need.

Passport and status paperwork. Keep copies in more than one place. You will be asked for ID constantly in the first month: for leases, phone plans, banks, and sometimes building access.

Lease or proof of address. Banks, utilities, and some government processes ask for proof that you live where you say you live. Founders in short-term rentals sometimes find this harder than expected. Ask early what your landlord or host can provide in writing.

SSN or ITIN. This comes up as a peer operations note, not advice. Some people are eligible for a Social Security number based on their status. Others who are not may need an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number for certain tax purposes. Which one applies to you, and when, depends on your facts. Start at the IRS ITIN page and the Social Security Administration number and card page. If you are unsure which applies, that is a question for a professional.

Company documents, separate from personal ones. Formation papers, EIN confirmation, and operating or governance documents belong to the company track. Peers suggest keeping them in their own folder so you are not digging through lease PDFs during a bank call.

Local operations

Getting around. Austin is spread out. Some founders downtown get by on walking, rideshare, and public transit for a while. Others decide quickly that they need a car, which brings its own questions about licenses and insurance. Check official Texas sources for licensing rules that apply to your situation rather than relying on what worked for a friend.

Phone and utilities. A US phone number early on helps with almost everything, from two-factor codes to landlord calls. Utility setup depends on your building and address, so ask your landlord what is already included.

A place to work. Many international founders use Station Austin at 701 Brazos St for coworking, especially in the first months when home is not set up yet. You also end up around other founders, which matters when you do not know anyone yet.

Getting to the IFN meetup. The IFN monthly in-person meetup for international and immigrant founders happens at Station Austin. Newcomers who come in their first month or two tend to find the landing goes faster, because they can ask about a landlord, a bank, or a document problem and usually find someone who has dealt with it.

When we stop talking

Call licensed professionals when any of these show up:

  • Immigration status questions, including what your visa allows you to do with your company, travel plans, and timing
  • Housing discrimination or lease disputes that escalate beyond peer tips
  • Tax residency questions: when you become a US tax resident, how that interacts with your home country, and how it affects your company

Immigration counsel, a housing or civil attorney when needed, and a CPA with cross-border experience are different seats.

Soft next steps

Come to the next IFN meetup with one concrete landing question: a neighborhood you are weighing, a document a bank asked for, or a lease decision you are stuck on. Guests are welcome; register on Luma or check dates on ifn.community. If you want the private member channel and members-only call, Become a member. Fuller relocation checklists and city notes live with membership and the Resources hub as that catalog fills in.

Sources

  • IRS, Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN)
  • Social Security Administration, Social Security number and card
  • Station Austin, stationaustin.org

forming-a-us-company-from-abroad.title: Forming a US company from abroad: what peers actually sequence
forming-a-us-company-from-abroad.description: What international founders at IFN Austin tend to sequence when forming a US company from abroad, and when they stop and call counsel.
forming-a-us-company-from-abroad.html:
At almost every IFN Austin meetup, someone still abroad asks the same cluster: Can I form a United States company before I have work authorization? LLC or C-corp? Which state? When does the EIN happen? How do people avoid confusing formation with permission to work?

This is peer sequencing from that room. Not a filing checklist. Not a substitute for counsel.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, tax, immigration, or banking advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. Entity choice, tax elections, beneficial ownership reporting, and immigration consequences change with your facts. Verify with licensed professionals and official sources (IRS, your state filing office, FinCEN) before you act.

Three tracks peers try to keep separate

Forming a US company is not the same as being authorized to work in the United States.

Founders who have been through it often separate three tracks early:

  1. Company paper (entity, registered agent, EIN, ownership docs)
  2. Personal status (visa, work authorization, travel)
  3. Money rails (banking, payments, how customers pay)

Mixing those tracks is where people get surprised. Formation can happen while you are still abroad. Work authorization is a different conversation. Banking prep is another. Meetup peers talk about all three; counsel owns the hard calls on each.

What people tend to sequence (high level)

No two founders run the same order. A pattern still shows up often enough that newcomers ask for it:

  1. Decide what job the entity has to do in the next 12 to 24 months (raise, serve US customers from abroad, support a later visa conversation without inventing eligibility, or keep a simple operating company). Peer pattern talk, not a recommendation. Cooley's June 2025 note on US visas and corporate structure is useful orientation; your advisors still own the call.

  2. Pick a formation state as an ops decision, not a brand decision. Delaware shows up because investors and counsel know it. Other states show up for cost or stack. Texas shows up when people already live or plan to live in Austin. Consistency with what you later show banks matters more than the logo on the filing. Delaware's Division of Corporations publishes how to form a new business entity; your own state's filing office is the source for non-Delaware filings.

  3. File, freeze the legal name, then get an EIN. Banks and the IRS notice character-level name mismatches. Founders abroad often learn online EIN eligibility depends on US presence and a suitable taxpayer ID for the responsible party. Start at the IRS EIN overview and Form SS-4 instructions.

  4. Keep ownership clear, and check current FinCEN BOI rules for your facts. Rules have changed. Start at FinCEN BOI reporting and FAQs, then ask counsel whether your facts still create a filing duty.

  5. Only then move toward banking. Incomplete company paper is an expensive way to learn. Peers gather formation evidence, EIN confirmation, ownership clarity, and a real operating address before they apply. The item-by-item pack language lives deeper with membership and Resources, not in this orientation post.

LLC vs C-corp as founders discuss it

In meetup language, LLCs get described as lighter early governance. Delaware C-corps get described as the default language for US venture conversations. Tax elections are not peer DIY. Structure and equity can interact with visa strategy, so corporate and immigration counsel often need to coordinate.

When we stop talking

Call licensed professionals when any of these show up:

  • You need a recommendation on LLC versus C-corp for your personal tax residency
  • Equity, vesting, or board control might interact with a visa strategy
  • You are unsure whether FinCEN BOI still applies to your entity
  • A formation service's marketing copy conflicts with IRS or state instructions
  • You are treating company formation as proof you can work in the US

Corporate counsel, immigration counsel, and a CPA who has worked with non-resident founders are different seats.

Soft next steps

Come to the next IFN meetup with one concrete formation question. Guests are welcome; register on Luma or check dates on ifn.community. If you want the private member channel and members-only call, Become a member. Fuller formation checklists and teaser PDFs live with membership and the Resources hub as that catalog fills in.

Sources

  • IRS, Employer identification number
  • IRS, Instructions for Form SS-4
  • Delaware Division of Corporations, How to form a new business entity
  • FinCEN, Beneficial Ownership Information Reporting
  • FinCEN, BOI FAQs
  • Cooley, What Foreign Founders Need to Know About US Visas and Corporate Structure (orientation; not IFN advice)

fundraising-as-an-international-founder-.title: Fundraising as an international founder: what changes in the US conversation
fundraising-as-an-international-founder-.description: Status, team location, and market narrative show up in US diligence. Peer prep from the IFN Austin room, not a pitch template.
fundraising-as-an-international-founder-.html:
Two founders are comparing notes at a corner table during an IFN meetup. One has just finished a round of calls with US angels. The other raised a seed round back home two years ago and is preparing for a US round now. The first one says the investor conversations went fine until about minute twenty, when the questions moved away from the product. "Where do you live? Who is on payroll? What happens if you cannot get back into the country?" The second founder nods and starts writing things down.

This is peer prep from that room: what tends to come up when international founders raise in the US, and how people prepare for it. Not a pitch template. Not an investor list. Not legal guidance.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, securities, tax, immigration, or financial advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. Every raise and every founder's status is different. Verify with licensed professionals and official sources before you act.

What changes compared with raising abroad

Founders who have raised in other markets often describe the US conversation as familiar on the surface and different underneath.

The metrics questions are similar everywhere: traction, retention, market size, team. What changes is how much attention goes to the structure around the founders. US investors who do not often back international founders can be more careful about status, location, and company setup. They may not say so directly. The questions just keep coming back to those areas.

Founders who have talked with non-US angels, or with angels from their own diaspora, often notice that those investors took certain things for granted. A US investor without that context may ask about them all at once. That is not necessarily a bad sign. It is usually an investor trying to understand a risk they have not had to think about before.

Status questions that show up

These questions come up in the room again and again. Peers share them as orientation so you are not surprised, not as a guide to answering them.

  • Work authorization. Investors may ask what your current status allows you to do in relation to the company, and whether that changes after a raise.
  • Travel risk. Some ask what happens if a founder cannot re-enter the US for a stretch, or has to leave for a renewal process.
  • Who can be on payroll. Questions about which founders and early employees can be paid by the US entity, and from where.

The pattern founders describe is simple. Know your own situation well enough to explain it calmly, and have counsel behind you for the details. When a founder can say their current status, what immigration counsel has advised, and the plan if it changes, investors tend to move on. When a founder guesses, the conversation tends to stall.

Peers are clear about one thing: questions about how a raise interacts with your status belong with an immigration attorney before you are in the investor meeting, not after.

Team location and the Austin story

Many international founders run teams spread across their home country, the US, and sometimes a third place. Investors will ask where the team sits and why.

Founders who have handled this well tend to describe the setup as it actually is. Engineering might be in one country, the founder and early go-to-market might be in Austin, and here is how the time zones work. Peers say a clear, real arrangement goes over better than an attempt to look more local than you are.

The room is skeptical of local-presence theater: a virtual address with nobody behind it, or claiming Austin as headquarters when nobody spends meaningful time there. Investors who do diligence tend to find out, and it costs credibility you need later.

Market narrative: why the US, why Austin

Investors want to know why US customers, and why now. Founders who come from strong home markets sometimes treat the US as the obvious next step without explaining it.

Peers who have been through it suggest grounding the story in evidence: US customers you already have, conversations with US buyers, or a specific reason your product fits this market. "Why Austin" works the same way. If you are here because your customers, your partners, or your co-founder are here, say that. If it is mainly because you like the city, that is fine too, but it does not make a market argument on its own.

Diligence documents peers gather

When a raise gets serious, investors and their counsel ask for documents. Founders who have been through it say the scramble is much smaller if a few things are in order before the first meeting. At a high level, the areas that come up are:

  • Company paper: formation documents, governance records, and anything showing the entity is in good standing
  • Cap table clarity: who owns what, whether earlier rounds or agreements from your home market are reflected cleanly, and whether any founder equity questions are still open
  • Banking readiness: a working US business account that can receive funds, plus a clear picture of how money moves between entities if you have more than one

The item-by-item pack language lives deeper with membership and Resources, not in this orientation post.

How peers actually prep

A few habits come up repeatedly in the room:

  • Run a practice conversation with a peer who has raised in the US and ask them to press hard on status and location
  • Write down your own one-paragraph explanation of your status, team setup, and company structure, then check it with counsel
  • Get your cap table and company records cleaned up before the first meeting
  • Talk to other international founders who raised from the investors you are approaching. Some investor groups focus specifically on immigrant founders. Ask peers who have direct experience before you go in.

When we stop talking

Call licensed professionals when any of these show up:

  • You need securities counsel for the raise itself: instruments, terms, and compliance with securities law
  • Equity, vesting, or board control might interact with a visa strategy
  • Cross-border tax questions on founder compensation, entity structure, or how the raise affects companies in more than one country
  • Someone offers you a "guaranteed" raise path tied to a visa story in a group chat

Securities counsel, immigration counsel, and a CPA who has worked with non-resident founders are different seats. Coordinate them early when a raise and a status plan are moving at the same time.

Soft next steps

Come to the next IFN meetup with one concrete fundraising prep question, such as a status question you expect from investors or a cap table issue you are unsure how to explain. Guests are welcome; register on Luma or check dates on ifn.community. If you want the private member channel and members-only call, Become a member. Fuller diligence prep lives with membership and the Resources hub as that catalog fills in.

Sources

This post is peer prep from the IFN Austin room. For anything tied to your specific status, securities, or tax position, go to qualified counsel and official government sources.

how-international-founders-find-us-legal.title: How international founders find US legal counsel (and what peers ask first)
how-international-founders-find-us-legal.description: Which kind of lawyer or CPA fits which question, how peers at IFN Austin find them, and what they ask before signing.
how-international-founders-find-us-legal.html:
Austin's in-person meetups sometimes have a founder scrolling through three notes on their phone that all say roughly the same thing. One came from a bank call: have your attorney review the operating agreement. One came from a co-founder conversation about splitting equity. The third came from someone at the last meetup who heard about their visa plans and said, kindly, that they should talk to counsel first. The founder wants to know if that means one lawyer or three. A few people at the table answer at once. It is closer to three, plus a CPA.

Most IFN posts end by sending you to a professional. This one is about that handoff: which kind of help fits which question, how peers in the room found theirs, and what they asked before signing anything. It is peer orientation, and it does not replace the advice you are about to go find.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, tax, immigration, or financial advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. IFN does not refer founders to, or endorse, any specific law firm, CPA, or advisor. Licensing rules and professional standards change, and the right fit depends on your facts. Verify with official sources and make your own choice.

Different seats, different questions

The mistake newcomers describe most often is asking one professional to cover everything because they already have that person's number.

Immigration counsel handles what your status allows: whether you can work for your own company, how ownership and role affect a petition, travel timing, and changes of status.

Corporate or startup counsel handles the company: entity choice, founder equity, investor documents, and contracts.

Employment counsel comes in when you hire, especially your first US employee or contractors in other countries.

A CPA with cross-border experience covers tax for both you and the company. Peers stress the cross-border part. A CPA who does good work for local small businesses may never have filed what a foreign-owned company needs.

A home-country advisor sometimes matters as much as anyone in Austin, particularly if your home country taxes worldwide income or has its own rules for a foreign company you control.

These seats do not substitute for each other. A good startup lawyer will often say plainly that your visa question is outside their lane, and peers read that as a good sign.

How peers find them

Most people in the room started with founders a step or two ahead. A useful referral is specific: what did that lawyer handle for you, what status were you on, and how did it go when something got complicated. "They're great" tells you less than a specific story, like a lawyer who spotted an equity problem before a petition went in.

The meetup room helps before you even have names. Describe what you are trying to do, and people can usually tell you which seat you need. That narrows the search.

Some founders first meet professionals through programs at Station Austin. A short conversation at an event is a low-pressure way to hear how someone explains things.

Then comes the official check. Before a first paid meeting, peers confirm the person is licensed. The State Bar of Texas has a public lawyer search on its website where you can confirm a Texas license and see public discipline history. Immigration lawyers may be licensed in another state and still practice federal immigration law, so peers check the bar in the state where the lawyer says they are licensed. For CPAs, the Texas State Board of Public Accountancy is the licensing body.

What peers ask in a first call

Founders who felt good about their choice usually asked a few plain questions early. Who the advisor usually represents. Whether they have worked with founders on a similar status. How billing works and who does the work day to day.

Peers pay attention to whether the answers come back plain or slippery. Fuller first-call notes and ways to compare advisors live with membership and the Resources hub.

Getting your advisors to talk to each other

People say they learned this part late. How much of the company you own, your title, who pays you, and where the entity is formed can all touch your status. Immigration and corporate questions overlap more than newcomers expect.

Before a raise, an entity change, a new co-founder, or a shift in your own role, people in the room suggest putting immigration counsel and corporate counsel on the same thread. Copy your CPA when money or ownership moves. If you are still at the formation stage, Forming a US company from abroad covers what peers sequence first.

You may end up as the messenger. Peers in that seat keep a short running note of what each advisor said and when, so they are not passing along decisions from memory.

Red flags peers mention

Guaranteed outcomes. Nobody can promise a visa approval. Peers treat a guarantee as a reason to keep looking.

"Notario" style services. In some countries a notary is a legal professional. In the US, a notary public is not a lawyer. USCIS warns about people who are not attorneys or accredited representatives offering immigration help. Peers point newcomers to the USCIS page on avoiding scams before they hand anyone their documents.

Pressure to sign the same day. A good advisor gives you time to read an engagement letter. If the urgency comes from the advisor and not from your own deadline, peers treat that as a reason to pause.

Vague answers about who will handle your file, or reluctance to put scope in writing, come up too.

Talking about cost

Many founders come from places where you do not ask a professional about fees up front. In the US people expect you to ask.

The two billing models you hear about most are flat fees and hourly billing. A flat fee covers a defined piece of work and is predictable as long as the scope holds. Hourly billing fits open-ended work where nobody can say in advance how long it will take. Some advisors also ask for a retainer, paid up front and drawn down as the work happens.

Peers suggest asking what is included, what counts as out of scope, and how you will hear about extra charges before they start. Then check that the engagement letter says the same thing the phone call did.

When we stop talking

This whole post sits at one moment: when a peer tip turns into a decision about your status, your company, or your taxes. That is where the room steps back. Bring in licensed help when:

  • An action could affect your immigration status, including starting work, changing your role, or travel
  • You are issuing equity, taking investment, or changing your entity
  • You are hiring your first employee or engaging contractors abroad
  • You need to know when you become a US tax resident or how your home country treats your company
  • Something has already gone wrong: a government notice, a dispute, or a document you signed without review

When a firm name comes up at a meetup, treat it as one founder's story and do your own checking. Peers can help you work out which kind of professional to call. They cannot stand in for that call.

Soft next steps

Come to the next IFN meetup with one concrete counsel question: which kind of advisor you need, how to check a license, or how to get two advisors aligned before a big change. Guests are welcome; register on Luma or check dates on ifn.community. If you want the private member channel and members-only call, Become a member. Fuller notes on choosing and working with advisors live with membership and the Resources hub as that catalog fills in.

Sources

  • Texas State Board of Public Accountancy, tsbpa.texas.gov
  • USCIS, Avoid Scams
  • Station Austin, stationaustin.org

how-we-validate-a-us-market-before-landi.title: How we validate a US market before landing
how-we-validate-a-us-market-before-landi.description: Customer discovery and research founders at IFN Austin do from abroad, without fake local presence, before they book the trip.
how-we-validate-a-us-market-before-landi.html:
Every so often a founder at the Austin meetup explains that they flew in for a week of "validation." They have a hotel near downtown, a deck on their laptop, and a plan to talk to customers. Someone asks how many calls they have booked, and the answer is none yet. They were hoping the city would take care of that part. A few people around the table nod, because they tried the same thing and spent most of that week in coffee shops refreshing their inbox.

This is peer orientation from that room. It covers how founders test a US market while still living somewhere else, what they avoid pretending, and when an Austin trip is worth what it costs. It is not a customer discovery course, and it does not replace counsel.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, tax, immigration, or business advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. What you can do on a visit, how a contract binds you, and when revenue creates tax obligations all depend on your facts. Verify with licensed professionals and official sources before you act.

Most of the work happens before the flight

Founders who did this well describe a boring pattern. They spent weeks or months on video calls from home before they bought a ticket.

Those calls were with people who might actually buy: operators, managers, and owners in the specific niche, based in the US, who have the problem the product claims to solve. Peers find them through their existing network, warm intros from earlier customers, industry groups, and sometimes plain cold outreach that says clearly who they are and why they are asking. Time zones are the real cost. A lot of people in the room have taken US calls at odd hours for months.

Alongside the conversations, people read what is public. The US Census Bureau publishes business data that gives you a rough sense of how many firms exist in an industry and where they cluster. It will not tell you whether anyone wants your product. It can stop you from building a plan around a market that is smaller than you assumed.

They also watch how US competitors sell. They look at pricing pages, how a free trial is framed, whether a sales call comes before anyone sees a price, and which job titles show up in case studies. None of that requires being in the country. It does require looking closely and noticing where US buyers seem to expect something different from buyers at home.

The questions peers come back to in early calls are simple. How does the buyer handle the problem today? What does it cost them when it goes wrong? Who else would have to say yes?

The fake local presence trap

The room is most direct about this part.

Some founders try to look local before they are. They list a virtual address as an "Austin office," get a US phone number that rings into a voicemail nobody checks, or build a website that implies a team in Texas when the whole team is abroad. The thinking is that US buyers will trust a local company more.

Buyers notice. They see it when a meeting invite comes from a time zone twelve hours away, when the "office" is a mailbox address they can look up, or when nobody answers the phone. Once that happens, the conversation moves away from your product and onto whether you are being straight with them.

Peers say it works better to state what is true: "We're based in Singapore, we work with US customers, and we're opening in Austin." Plenty of US buyers are fine working with a company abroad. Far fewer are fine finding out that a company misrepresented itself. A registered agent or a mailing service is a legitimate tool for company paperwork. The trouble starts when you present it as a place where people work.

If you have already formed the US entity, the post on forming a US company from abroad covers how peers sequence that side. Formation and presence are separate questions.

Signals the room treats as real

Founders who have been through a few cycles sort feedback roughly into two piles.

Weak signals include likes on a post about the idea, survey answers saying "I would use this," compliments at the end of a call, and people agreeing that the problem exists. These feel good and tell you little.

Stronger signals look more like this:

  • A buyer agrees to a paid pilot, even a small one
  • Someone asks for a second call and brings a colleague
  • A contact forwards your intro to someone else without being chased
  • A prospect starts asking about contract terms, security, or billing

What the stronger signals share is cost. Each one asks the buyer to spend money, time, or some of their reputation. If nobody has done any of that yet, peers usually suggest more calls before more travel.

A status note

This comes up as a peer note, not advice. Under immigration rules, talking with potential customers during a US visit and actually doing work in the US can be different questions. Where one ends and the other begins depends on your status and on what you do during the trip. Founders in the room have been surprised by how fine that line can be, and a discovery meeting and delivering paid work on site may not be treated the same way.

Peers usually start with the USCIS page on B-1 business visitors and our post on visa paths founders talk about at IFN, which covers what the room discusses and where we hand off. Founders who travel for discovery say they talked to immigration counsel before the trip, not after.

Where the Austin trip fits

Once you have real signals, a trip starts to make sense. Peers describe it as a way to pressure-test what the calls already suggested.

A useful week usually has meetings booked before you land. These can be in-person follow-ups with people who already took a video call, perhaps a visit to a pilot customer, and time with founders who sell to the same kind of buyer. Austin helps with that last part. Many international founders work out of Station Austin at 701 Brazos St, and the IFN monthly meetup for international and immigrant founders happens there. If you bring your signals to that room, along with what you are unsure about, problems tend to come up faster than they would with another week of desk research.

Peers try not to let the trip stand in for the work. An empty calendar in Austin teaches you very little.

When we stop talking

Peer notes stop and licensed help starts when:

  • You are planning a US trip and are not sure what your status allows you to do while you are there, including meetings, pilots, or anything that looks like work
  • A US customer sends you a contract, pilot agreement, or data terms to sign. Peers have counsel read it first.
  • Revenue from US customers starts arriving and you need to understand the tax obligations for the entity and for you personally. That is a job for a CPA, ideally one with cross-border experience.

Immigration counsel, a business attorney, and a CPA are different seats. It is rare for one person to cover all three well.

Soft next steps

Come to the next IFN meetup with one concrete validation question: a signal you are not sure how to read, a pricing pattern you noticed, or a trip you are deciding whether to book. Guests are welcome; register on Luma or check dates on ifn.community. If you want the private member channel and members-only call, Become a member. Fuller discovery guides and market research notes live with membership and the Resources hub as that catalog fills in.

Sources

  • US Census Bureau, census.gov
  • USCIS, B-1 Temporary Business Visitor
  • Station Austin, stationaustin.org

money-questions-to-sort-before-you-land-.title: Money questions international founders sort before they land in the US
money-questions-to-sort-before-you-land-.description: Credit from zero, moving money, keeping company money separate, and home-country ties: what peers at IFN Austin wish they sorted before landing.
money-questions-to-sort-before-you-land-.html:
Someone at the IFN Austin meetup usually has a version of this story. They went into a phone store expecting a simple monthly plan and came out with a request for a deposit. A week later, the apartment they wanted asked for a deposit too, and suggested a guarantor they did not have. Back home they had years of clean credit, loans paid on time, and a bank that knew them by name. None of it counted here. The founder next to them nods, because the same thing happened to them in their first month.

This is peer orientation from that room: the money questions founders wish they had worked through before boarding the plane. It won't replace a financial plan, and it isn't a checklist to run line by line.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, tax, immigration, investment, or banking advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. Credit rules, reporting thresholds, tax residency, and transfer regulations change, and they depend on your facts and your home country. Verify with licensed professionals and official sources before you act.

The questions worth answering before you fly

When peers look back, the money surprises tend to land in a few places: credit from zero, moving money across borders, keeping personal and company money apart, what still lives back home, and what the move itself costs. What follows is how the room talks about each. Fuller pre-arrival notes live with membership and Resources.

Credit starts at zero

The thing most newcomers find hardest to accept is that a strong credit record at home usually does not follow you. US lenders, landlords, and phone carriers check US credit reports, and when you first arrive you have no file there at all. To them you look the same as someone who has never borrowed anything.

Founders describe building it slowly and on purpose. A pattern that comes up often is a secured card, where a deposit backs a small limit and on-time payments slowly build a US history. A few people mention services that claim to bring foreign credit history across. Results in the room have been mixed, so peers ask around before counting on one.

Many applications ask for an SSN or ITIN, which ties credit building back to the identity paperwork from your first weeks. Peers also suggest checking your own report once a file exists, partly to catch errors and partly to understand what lenders actually see. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau at consumerfinance.gov has plain explanations of credit reports, scores, and how to dispute mistakes.

Peers plan for deposits and slower approvals in the first months. It happens to most new arrivals and says nothing about you.

Moving money across borders

Most founders in the room have moved money internationally, and many have a story about a transfer that cost more or took longer than expected.

Exchange costs hide in the rate. Beyond any visible fee, there is often a gap between the market exchange rate and the rate you actually receive. On a large transfer, that gap can matter more than the fee. Peers compare the amount that lands, not the advertised fee.

Timing is slower than you think. International transfers can take days, and a first large transfer may trigger extra review on either end. Some home countries also have rules or limits on moving money out. Founders who needed funds for a lease deposit on a specific date learned to send early.

Records matter later. Peers save the confirmation for each transfer with a short note on why the money moved. Later, a CPA, a bank compliance team, or sometimes an immigration filing may ask where money came from. Rebuilding that trail a year later is miserable.

Personal money and company money

The room is close to unanimous on this one: do not mix them.

The company account follows formation, because banks will want formation documents and an EIN before they open it. If you are still in that stage, US business banking for international founders: what peers gather first covers what people pull together. Until the company account is open, some founders end up paying early company costs personally. Peers who did this and kept receipts were fine. Peers who did not spent a weekend untangling a card statement before their first tax filing.

How money goes from you into the company also matters. Founder loans, capital contributions, and reimbursements are treated differently, and the right structure depends on your situation. That is a CPA conversation. The peer habit is simpler: write down every movement between your personal accounts and the company's, as it happens.

The home-country side does not disappear

Leaving a country does not automatically end your obligations there. Founders mention bank accounts that need to stay active, loans still being repaid, property, pensions, and family support they send regularly. Some home countries continue to treat you as a tax resident for a period after you leave, or based on ties you keep.

A small practical note that comes up more than you would expect: many home-country banks send login codes to your home phone number. People who let that number lapse have been locked out of their own accounts from Austin. Peers sort out how they will keep access before they leave.

Peers who had a smooth first year usually had a CPA in each country, and sometimes got the two talking to each other early.

US reporting for foreign accounts

This one gets a plain flag. The IRS describes a yearly reporting requirement for some US persons with financial accounts outside the US above certain thresholds, often called the FBAR. It explains the rules on its Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR) page.

Whether it applies to you, and from when, depends on your tax status and your accounts. That is a question for a CPA, and founders in the room are careful not to guess for each other.

Runway for the move itself

Founders often budget carefully for the company and forget that the move has its own cost. Short-term housing while you look, lease and utility deposits, phone deposits from that opening story, furniture, transport, and professional fees for formation, tax, and immigration help all arrive in the first months. Some people pay rent in two cities for a stretch.

The pattern peers suggest is to keep a separate number for landing costs, so the company's runway is not quietly eaten by your personal setup. Bring your actual estimate to a meetup. People who landed recently will tell you what they forgot.

When we stop talking

Bring in licensed help when any of these show up:

  • Tax residency in either country, foreign account reporting, how you fund the company, and how you pay yourself: a CPA with cross-border experience
  • Investments, pensions, or moving larger sums between countries: a financial advisor licensed in the relevant country
  • Any situation where proof of funds or source of funds matters for your status: immigration counsel (the room's limits here are in Visa paths founders talk about at IFN)

These are different seats, and one person rarely covers all of them.

Soft next steps

Come to the next IFN meetup with one concrete money question: a deposit you were asked for, a transfer you are planning, or a home-country account you are unsure about keeping. Guests are welcome; register on Luma or check dates on ifn.community. If you want the private member channel and members-only call, Become a member. Fuller pre-arrival financial checklists and credit-building notes live with membership and the Resources hub as that catalog fills in.

Sources

  • Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, consumerfinance.gov
  • IRS, Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR)

opening-an-ein-and-why-the-letter-matter.title: Opening an EIN and why the letter matters for banking
opening-an-ein-and-why-the-letter-matter.description: Why banks ask for the IRS EIN letter, where name mismatches stall applications, and how peers at IFN Austin keep the paper straight.
opening-an-ein-and-why-the-letter-matter.html:
A familiar moment at the IFN Austin meetup: a founder scrolls back through their inbox to show the table an email with a nine-digit number in it. That's their EIN. Their business bank application has been in review for two weeks, and the bank's latest message asked for "the IRS letter." They have the number but not the letter, and they aren't sure which letter the bank means. Two people across the table nod, because the same thing held up their accounts.

This is peer orientation from that room: what an EIN is, why banks care so much about the paper behind it, and where it tends to fit in the order of things. Not a filing guide. Not tax advice.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, tax, immigration, or banking advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. IRS processes, letter names, and bank requirements change, and the right answer depends on your entity, your ownership, and your status. Verify with licensed professionals and official sources before you act.

What an EIN is, plainly

An Employer Identification Number is a nine-digit number the IRS assigns to a business for federal tax purposes. Plenty of companies with no employees have one, mostly because banks, payment processors, payroll providers, and larger customers ask for it before they will work with you.

The IRS explains who needs one and how to apply on its Get an Employer Identification Number page. Form SS-4 is the underlying application. The About Form SS-4 page has the current form and instructions. Peers read those directly. IRS pages change, and the source beats a forwarded screenshot.

When you have no SSN or ITIN

This is where many international founders first get stuck. The IRS online application expects the person listed as responsible for the company to have a Social Security number or ITIN, and it is only for companies whose principal place of business is in the US. A lot of people in the room had no SSN or ITIN when they formed.

The path they describe is a paper Form SS-4 sent by fax or mail, and it takes longer than the online flow. Founders whose principal place of business is outside the US also mention the IRS phone line for international applicants. The paper comes back differently too: the IRS says a fax application usually gets the number back by fax in about four business days, and mail takes about four weeks. Which channels are open, and how long each takes, changes. Peers check the IRS EIN page at the time they apply instead of relying on how someone did it last year.

Some founders hand this step to a formation service or an accountant. That can save time. Founders who go that route say one extra question up front helps: how will the IRS document itself reach you, along with the number? Founders who skipped that question often end up holding exactly what the person in the opening scene had, a number in an email.

The letter behind the number

Peers mention two documents most often.

The first is the notice the IRS issues when it assigns the number, the CP575. Depending on how you applied, it may come by mail some weeks later, or it may be available to save at the end of an online session. A few founders who applied online found that saving it was easy to miss in the moment. The IRS says the original notice cannot be duplicated, so a lost one means asking for a different document.

The second is Letter 147C, which the IRS calls "EIN Previously Assigned." Founders tend to ask for it by phone when the original notice is lost, or when a bank or processor wants confirmation that matches the company's current details. The IRS now offers a digital EIN verification notice, confusingly also named CP575, inside its Business Tax Account, and says banks accept it in place of a 147C. Not every founder can use that account. Letter names and options change, so peers check the IRS EIN page before asking.

Banks ask for this paper because they're matching records. During onboarding they compare the legal name, the EIN, and often the address against your formation documents and the IRS record. A number typed into an email from a vendor shows that someone has a number. An IRS document shows the IRS issued it to that exact entity.

Where the name match breaks

Most of the stalled applications people describe come down to small differences.

The company is "Example Labs, LLC" on the state filing and "Example Labs LLC" on the EIN notice, partly because IRS systems only accept a short list of characters in business names. Or the suffix got dropped. Or someone applied for the EIN under a trade name instead of the legal name. To a person these look identical. Some bank review processes treat them as a mismatch, and the application waits until someone sorts it out.

Responsible party issues come up too, at a higher level. The IRS expects a real individual who controls the entity to be listed. Founders have hit trouble when the person on the EIN record isn't the person opening the account, when a co-founder listed at formation has since left, or when nobody is quite sure who was entered. The IRS has a process for reporting changes (Form 8822-B, and the IRS says responsible party changes are due within 60 days). Whether you need it, and how it interacts with your ownership, is a question for a CPA, not the meetup table.

The pattern peers repeat: read the EIN document against your formation papers character by character before you start any bank or processor application. It takes a few minutes and can save weeks in a review queue.

Where it sits in the sequence

In the order most founders describe, the entity exists first, the EIN comes next, and banking comes after that. People who applied for an EIN before the state approved the final company name sometimes created the very mismatch they later had to unwind.

For more on the formation side, Forming a US company from abroad covers what peers sequence before the EIN. For the bank side, US business banking for international founders covers the rest of the document pack banks tend to request.

Where peers keep the letter

Founders who settled in smoothly usually treat company paper as its own track, separate from personal landing and from money movement. The EIN document belongs with the formation papers and governance documents, in a company folder that isn't mixed in with lease PDFs and passport scans.

Peers keep a clean digital copy and know where the original is. Some also note how and when they applied, because that context helps if they ever request a verification letter. Processors, banks, and investors can ask for the document again long after formation.

When we stop talking

Peer notes run out quickly on this topic. Bring in licensed help when any of these come up:

  • Tax classification and elections. How your entity is taxed, whether any election makes sense, and what reporting applies to a foreign-owned company. A CPA with cross-border experience is the right seat for this.
  • Responsible party questions. Who should be listed, what happens when that person changes, and how to correct the record.
  • Correcting a name or record mismatch with the IRS, especially when a bank or investor is waiting on it.
  • Complex ownership. A parent company abroad, founders in several countries, investors, or nominee arrangements. That is corporate counsel territory before anything gets filed.
  • Status questions. What your visa allows you to do inside the company is a question for immigration counsel.

Soft next steps

Come to the next IFN meetup with one concrete EIN or banking question: a letter you can't find, a name that doesn't quite match, or a bank request you don't understand. Guests are welcome; register on Luma or check dates on ifn.community. If you want the private member channel and members-only call, Become a member. Fuller company paperwork notes and banking prep live with membership and the Resources hub as that catalog fills in.

Sources

  • IRS, Get an Employer Identification Number
  • IRS, About Form SS-4, Application for Employer Identification Number
  • IRS, Employer identification number
  • IRS, Understanding your CP575 notice
  • IRS, Instructions for Form SS-4

us-business-banking-document-pack.title: US business banking for international founders: what peers gather first
us-business-banking-document-pack.description: What international founders at IFN tend to gather before they walk into a US business banking conversation, at overview level.
us-business-banking-document-pack.html:
After formation and EIN talk, banking is the next wall at IFN Austin meetups. Founders often say they assumed the hard part was "being foreign." What they describe afterward sounds more like incomplete company paper: mismatched names, a registered-agent address used as the operating address, missing EIN confirmation, or ownership docs that do not match passport spellings.

This is peer orientation on what people tend to gather before they walk into a bank or remote onboarding flow. It is not a downloadable checklist, not a promise any bank will approve you, and not product endorsement. The fuller pack language belongs with membership and Resources.

Disclaimer

This is not banking, legal, tax, or immigration advice. Bank and fintech policies change. Underwriting is individual. Verify requirements with the institution you apply to. IFN shares patterns from founder conversations, not guarantees.

The wrong wall, in meetup language

A common story in the room: form a US LLC or C-corp from abroad, upload a passport and Articles PDF to a remote business account, get stalled or declined, then conclude "US banks do not want internationals."

Peers who cleared remote onboarding usually rewrite that story: the underwriter could not reconcile an incomplete company file. Nationality still matters for some products. Incomplete paper fails more often than founders expect.

Industry examples (not IFN endorsements): Mercury's How to open a U.S. bank account remotely and OtoCo's 2026 foreign-owned LLC banking guide. Your bank's checklist still wins.

What peers tend to gather (overview, not a pack)

Every institution differs. At a high level, founders who later cleared onboarding usually had these categories ready before they applied:

  • Formation evidence with the exact legal name, state, and filing date. Entity choice and sequencing are a separate peer conversation; keep company paper frozen before you apply.
  • EIN confirmation that matches that legal name. IRS EIN overview and Form SS-4 instructions.
  • Ownership and signing authority clear enough that beneficial owners and control persons are not a mid-review surprise.
  • Government IDs for owners and control persons, with names that match formation docs.
  • A real business mailing or principal place of business address, separate from the registered agent used only for service of process. Many remote underwriters reject registered-agent-only or PO box-only addresses. Check yours.
  • A boring, true business description. Vague activity language creates manual review. Inventing a safer-sounding industry creates a worse problem later.

That is orientation, not a fillable inventory. The item-by-item pack and member-channel walkthroughs live deeper in Resources and with membership.

Remote path vs traditional path

Remote path: browser upload plus review. Peers report stalls when the address is the registered agent, the EIN name mismatches, beneficial ownership is incomplete, or the activity is unsupported.

Traditional path: denser KYC, longer timelines, sometimes an in-person step. Branch visits with Articles alone often burn the trip.

Product names come and go. Re-read current eligibility pages, including any prohibited-residence list, before you build plans on a forum thread.

SSN, ITIN, and a separate visa track

In many remote stories, the company is the customer and controlling persons provide passport KYC. An SSN is not always required for the company account. An ITIN is personal; it is not a substitute for the company's EIN. Some banks still want a US person with signing authority.

Visa status is a separate track. Owning a US company is not permission to work in the United States. Keep personal status questions for immigration counsel, not for the banking underwriter.

When we stop talking

Call a professional or the bank's support channel when:

  • You need a product recommendation for your facts
  • Your industry or residence may be unsupported
  • Names or addresses already conflict across docs
  • Someone suggests misstating activity to pass review
  • Tax residency or payroll setup enters the chat
  • A decline letter needs interpretation against your KYC file

Meetup peers can share what they assembled. They cannot underwrite you.

Soft next steps

Bring your banking-prep questions (not your passport data) to the next IFN meetup. Guests are welcome; register on Luma or check ifn.community. For the private member channel, members-only call, and the fuller banking pack / teaser PDF language as it ships, Become a member or browse Resources.
