us-go-to-market-when-your-product-was-bu.title: US go-to-market when your first product was built elsewhere
us-go-to-market-when-your-product-was-bu.description: How pricing conversations, trust signals, and early channels change when a product built abroad starts selling to US buyers.
us-go-to-market-when-your-product-was-bu.html:
A founder sits at the IFN meetup table with an email thread open on their laptop. At home, the product sells through referrals and a short demo, and most deals close inside a few calls. Here, a US prospect liked the demo and then sent back a list of questions. Is there a security review document? Do you have a US entity? Can we talk to two US customers? What support hours do you keep in Central time? None of these came up at home. The founder wants to know which one to answer first, and whether the deal is even real.

The room hears some version of this most months. This post is peer orientation on what tends to change when a product built in one market starts selling into the US: how pricing conversations shift, which trust signals buyers look for, and which channels founders say worked first. It is not a go-to-market playbook, and it does not replace counsel or a CPA.

Disclaimer

This is not legal, tax, immigration, or financial advice. IFN shares what founders in the room tend to talk through. Contract terms, privacy obligations, sales tax, and what your status allows you to do all depend on your facts. Verify with licensed professionals and official sources before you act.

Pricing conversations change shape

Founders rarely say their price was wrong. More often they say the way they presented it did not land.

US buyers, especially in B2B software, often expect clear packaging. That usually means a small number of tiers and a plain description of what each one includes. At home, a custom quote for every customer can work because relationships carry the sale. Here, it can feel like friction, or like a sign the product is not finished yet.

Annual versus monthly comes up a lot. Some buyers want monthly so they can try the product with less risk. Some finance teams prefer annual because it is easier to budget. Founders compare notes on which option they lead with and why. The room has no single answer. What peers suggest is deciding on purpose instead of copying the home model.

Currency gets less attention. If you quote in your home currency, or in a mix, the buyer has an extra step, and you can look like a vendor procurement has to set up specially. Most founders selling here end up quoting in US dollars. Then they have to work out how that money moves between the US entity and the team at home.

Sales tax is the one people find out about late. Depending on what you sell and where your buyers are, selling into US states can create obligations you did not plan for. The room raises the issue and stops there. It is CPA territory. For Texas specifically, the Texas Comptroller is the official place to start reading.

Trust signals US buyers ask for

When founders compare notes, the same requests come up across very different products.

A US entity and a US bank account. Procurement teams often want to pay a US company, into a US account, with a W-9 on file. A foreign entity can still close deals, but it adds questions at the worst point in the sale. Peers who sorted their banking early say it took one blocker out of every deal. The banking post covers what people gather first.

Contracts that look familiar to US buyers. If your agreement was drafted under home-country law with home-country conventions, the buyer's legal team may slow down or send back heavy redlines. Founders who had counsel review their customer terms for US buyers before they started selling say later deals moved faster. The room does not pass around contract language. That work belongs with a lawyer.

Support hours that overlap. Peers say round-the-clock coverage is rarely the ask. Buyers want to know which hours you cover in US time zones and what happens outside them. A buyer who knows you answer by mid-morning Central time is usually fine. A buyer who finds out by waiting is not.

References from US customers. Your first US customer counts for more than its revenue. Some founders ask early whether that customer would take a reference call later, and they keep the relationship warm so the answer stays yes. Logos from your home market still help, but many US buyers do not know them, so founders add a sentence of context.

A clear privacy and security posture. Security questionnaires show up earlier than most founders expect, sometimes before pricing does. Peers suggest having a plain description of how you handle customer data, where it is stored, and who can access it. Getting that description right for your product is a job for counsel. The FTC's business guidance is an official starting point for understanding how US regulators think about privacy and data security.

Say where the team is

Some founders admit they tried to look local at first: a US phone number, an Austin address on the website, and vague answers about where engineering sits. Most gave it up.

It usually comes out on the first scheduling call, when time zones show. A buyer who feels misled about something small starts to wonder what else is off. What works better is plain language: where the team is based, which hours you cover, and who the buyer's US contact is. Plenty of US buyers work with distributed teams every day. Surprises are what bother them.

Channels: what translated and what did not

Founders who got traction here describe a similar order, even if the timing varied.

Founder-led sales came first for nearly everyone. Early US conversations teach you what buyers misunderstand about your product, and you lose that if you hand sales off too soon. Warm intros came next. That is one reason people keep coming back to the meetup: someone in the room knows someone who buys what you sell. Niche communities in your industry, online and in person, often did more than general startup events. Partnerships with companies that already sell to your buyer helped some founders, though they usually took longer than expected.

Paid ads mostly came later. Founders who started with ads before they knew which message worked say they spent money and learned little.

On what translated from home, the answers are mixed:

  • Copy usually needed a rewrite. A straight translation rarely landed. Tone is often the gap: what reads as polite and thorough at home can read as slow or vague to a US buyer.
  • Spelling and formats matter more than people expect. British spelling, day-first dates, and metric-only specs tell a US reader the site was not written for them.
  • Case studies from home still carry weight when the problem is the same, but they need context a US reader can follow.
  • The core product usually traveled fine. What took the most work was the story around it.

When we stop talking

The room is useful for patterns. Bring in licensed help when any of these come up:

  • Customer contracts, terms of service, privacy policies, and data handling commitments: counsel who works with US commercial agreements
  • Sales tax, nexus, and revenue recognition for annual or multi-year contracts: a CPA, ideally one with cross-border experience
  • If you personally do sales, demos, or contract negotiation while you are in the US: immigration counsel, because what your status allows depends on your facts (the visa paths post covers where peer talk ends)

These are separate roles, and one professional rarely covers all of them.

Soft next steps

Come to the next IFN meetup with one concrete go-to-market question: a buyer request you have not seen before, a packaging decision you are stuck on, or a channel you are unsure about. Guests are welcome; register on Luma or check dates on ifn.community. The meetup happens at Station Austin. If you want the private member channel and members-only call, Become a member. Fuller go-to-market notes and buyer-readiness materials live with membership and the Resources hub as that catalog fills in.

Sources

  • Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts, comptroller.texas.gov
  • Federal Trade Commission, Business guidance
  • Station Austin, stationaustin.org

visa-paths-founders-talk-about-at-ifn.title: Visa paths founders talk about at IFN (and when we stop talking)
visa-paths-founders-talk-about-at-ifn.description: A peer map of visa paths founders discuss at IFN meetups, and the moments the room hands the conversation to immigration counsel.
visa-paths-founders-talk-about-at-ifn.html:
Visa questions arrive early at IFN Austin meetups. Someone is still on a student timeline. Someone else is abroad and wondering whether to form a company first. Someone on an employer-sponsored status asks what they can do for a side project without putting their status at risk.

This is a peer orientation map of the paths that come up in the room. IFN does not file petitions. IFN does not tell you which visa you qualify for.

Disclaimer

This is not immigration, legal, tax, or banking advice. USCIS, the Department of State, and licensed immigration counsel are the authorities for eligibility, petitions, and status decisions. Rules change. Your facts matter. Use this only as meetup-shaped orientation, then verify with professionals and official pages before you act.

How the room talks about visas

Founders at IFN tend to talk in paths and constraints:

  • What status am I on now?
  • What am I allowed to do for a company I own?
  • What would a change of status or a consular application require?
  • Who petitions: me, my company, an employer, or a family member?
  • When do I stop brainstorming and hire counsel?

Peer stories help you ask better questions. They do not replace a case assessment. A careful public overview is Cooley's June 2025 note on foreign founders, visas, and corporate structure. Read it as orientation. Your attorney still owns your case.

The room also compares notes on timing: when to talk to counsel relative to incorporation, fundraising, or a planned trip. That timing talk stays peer pattern. It is never a filing calendar.

Paths that come up often (names + official links only)

The names below are classifications founders discuss at meetups. Official pages are linked so you can read primary language yourself. IFN does not score eligibility or assemble evidence packages.

  • O-1. Comes up when founders have a dense record of recognition in a defined field. The moment anyone asks "do I have enough evidence?" the room stops. USCIS O-1.
  • E-2. Comes up for nationals of qualifying treaty countries, usually alongside investment and ownership questions that are fact-specific. Check the treaty list first. USCIS E-2, Treaty Countries.
  • H-1B. Comes up around lottery calendars, employer-specific limits, and founder-owned company questions. IFN does not draw that line. USCIS H-1B.
  • L-1. Comes up when there is already a real foreign operating company, not only an idea. USCIS L-1A, L-1B.
  • Student and visitor timelines (F-1, OPT, B-1/B-2). Ownership and active work are different questions. As soon as the question becomes "am I allowed to do X on my current status?" the meetup conversation ends.
  • Green card / EB conversations. Peer orientation only. Counsel early. No eligibility theater.

Formation and visas are linked, but not the same project

A recurring IFN lesson: people form a US company and then assume the visa problem is solved. It is not.

Company paper and personal status move on different clocks. Peers who stay calm tend to keep a written list of what their current status allows, form the entity only when it serves a clear ops or fundraising job, gather banking materials after the entity exists, and book immigration counsel before they restructure equity "for a visa story."

When we stop talking

Call immigration counsel when:

  • You want a recommendation among O-1, E-2, H-1B, L-1, or any other path
  • You need evidence strategy, petition drafting, or consular prep
  • Your nationality, dual citizenship, or prior refusals change the map
  • You are on student or visitor status and want a green light for active work
  • Equity, board control, or vesting might be rearranged for status reasons
  • Someone offers you a "guaranteed" petition path in a group chat

IFN is a peer room. Counsel is a licensed professional with your facts and your file.

Soft next steps

Bring one status question to the next IFN meetup. Guests stay free via the meetup; register on Luma or see dates on ifn.community. If you want the private member channel and members-only call, Become a member. Deeper visa pathway maps and teaser PDFs live with membership and Resources as that hub fills in.

welcome-to-the-ifn-blog.title: Welcome to the IFN blog
welcome-to-the-ifn-blog.description: Peer notes from IFN meetups in Austin for international founders. Field notes you can read before you walk into the room.
welcome-to-the-ifn-blog.html:
IFN runs a free monthly meetup in Austin for international and immigrant founders. The same questions show up every month: how people register a company in the United States, how they stay inside visa limits while they build, how they open a bank account, and how local funding conversations differ from the ones they had at home.

This blog is where we write those conversations down. Not legal advice. Not a course. Peer experience from founders who are doing the work in Austin, so you can arrive at the next meetup with sharper questions.

What you will find here

  • Field notes from the room: what surprised people who just landed, and what they wish they had asked earlier.
  • Orientation on visas, entity setup, banking, housing, hiring, and fundraising as an international founder, always as peer framing. When a topic needs counsel, we say so.
  • Soft pointers to the next meetup, the optional membership (private member channel and members-only call), and the Resources hub when a catalog title is useful.

What this is not

This is not the paid Resources library. Guides that belong behind membership stay there. The blog stays free to read.

It is also not a newsletter signup page. When we publish, the post lives at /blog. Come to a meetup if you want the live version of the same conversation.

Start here

If you are new to Austin as an international founder, come to the next meetup first. Register on Luma. Bring one concrete question. The blog will keep adding the written version of what the room keeps teaching.
